newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark firm on decision to use veto at EU meeting.
newsitem.headline: Denmark firm on decision to use veto at EU meeting.

text.p: Denmark plans on Monday to ignore appeals from other European Union members and veto a joint stand against U.S. anti-Cuba trade legislation, an aide to Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said on Saturday.

But she added that Petersen was expected to vote with his EU colleagues for a common intitiative against racism based on the same article of EU law which Denmark said it would not allow to be used in the bloc's fight against the U.S. Helms-Burton Act.
The votes will take place at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday and Tuesday in Luxembourg.

Copenhagen has said it shares other members' opposition to the controversial U.S. law, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy which allows Americans to sue foreigners or foreign companies profitting from Cuban property confiscated since the 1959 Communist revolution.

Petersen says his country's lone stand against EU countermeasures stems from the use of the catch-all clause 235 of the EU's founding treaties, which is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the EU bloc.

Danish officials say the veto will be cast on judicial, not political, grounds, but EU diplomats are convinced Denmark's reluctance to use clause 235 results from concern about the implications in an impending court hearing on the legality of EU treaties.
The Petersen aide said the decision to support the anti-racist package showed that this was not true.

"It only demonstrates that we are not so scared of this case in court that we are never willing to use 235," she said, adding there were complex legal reasons why Denmark saw the paragraph as applicable on the racism issue but not against Helms-Burton.

Preliminary hearings are to begin in a Copengagen court next Friday in a suit by 11 Danes alleging that some of Denmark's commitments under EU treaties violated constitutional guarantees of national sovereignty.

The Danish government believes that the legality of the treaties is unassailable, but legal experts say that it will have to tread with extreme caution on issues of sovereignty until the case is decided, possible after years in court.
The latest hiccup in the EU's attempts to act as a single cohesive group has highlighted the debate about whether more issues should be voted by majority rather than unanimity in the 15-nation bloc.
On Thursday, EU Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan urged Denmark to fall back into line with the bloc's other 14 members and said he saw a need for more decision-taking by qualified majority.

While Denmark's Social Democrat-led government is publicly pro-EU, its members have varying degrees of reservations. The public, which rocked the EU by rejecting Maastricht in a 1992 referendum, is decidely lukewarm.

Although the electorate grudgingly approved the accord in a second plebiscite a year later, it did so only on condition that Denmark stay out of Economic and Monetary Union and reject other clauses seen as a danger to national independence.
